extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and comedy studies; readers interested in theories of humor
extracted.subtask_description: Summarize and evaluate philosophical and psychological theories about what humor is, what produces laughter, and what makes particular bits/jokes amusing or objectionable. Includes theoretical criteria (incongruity, play, superiority), conversational mechanisms, ethical considerations, and social/psychological functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity (core)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some thing or event we perceive or think about violates our standard mental patterns and normal expectations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the core meaning of the Incongruity Theory: the comic arises when what is perceived conflicts with what is expected. Examples include jokes whose punch line violates the initial interpretation. Note that mere perception of incongruity is not sufficient for amusement (see related criteria).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity-resolution (enjoyment via fitting)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often depends not just on perceiving incongruity but on resolving it — 'the fitting of the apparently anomalous element into some conceptual schema' (Schultz).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the hearer reinterprets earlier material so it makes sense (e.g., Mae West’s 'institution' pun), amusement is akin to puzzle-solving. Unresolvable incongruity may be classified as 'nonsense' rather than humor. Use this to evaluate wordplay, puns, and many punchlines that require reinterpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three features of enjoyable incongruity (Michael Clark)
rubrics_metrics.description: For humor Clark proposes three necessary-and-sufficient features: (1) a person perceives an object as incongruous; (2) the person enjoys perceiving that incongruity; (3) the person enjoys the perceived incongruity at least partly for itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This refines the Incongruity Theory by adding enjoyment and self-contained appreciation as requirements; use these features to distinguish mere surprise or confusion from genuine humorous amusement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Affective context constraint (Beattie / counterexample to sufficiency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Perception of incongruity will not produce risible amusement when it is 'attended with some other emotion of greater authority' such as fear, pity, moral disapproval, indignation, or disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether an incongruity will be funny, check for competing strong emotions. If present, the response is likely fear, anger, or pity rather than laughter. Use this to judge appropriateness and likely audience reaction (e.g., dark/traumatic subjects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as abstract subsumption (Schopenhauer)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit 'consists entirely in a facility for finding for every object that appears a conception under which it certainly can be thought' — the ability to subsume very different things under a single abstract idea that makes their disparity funny.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion evaluates the intellectual cleverness of jokes that rely on conceptual shifts or high-level abstractions; examples include jokes that reveal a category-level mismatch. Assessors should look for a clear, illuminating abstraction that highlights disparity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play/Non-serious framing (humor as play)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor is a kind of play: a non-serious, pleasure-seeking activity that intentionally violates norms or expectations in a safe setting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the humorous act adopts a 'disinterested' or nonpractical attitude that treats violations playfully. This framing explains benefits (rest for the soul, stress reduction) and supports the idea that humor can be valuable rather than irrational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as play signal / sociality
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter and smiling function as play signals that mark an activity as non-serious; laughter is overwhelmingly social (we are far more likely to laugh with others than alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether performers/signals clearly mark playful intent (smile, laugh, play face) so recipients interpret behavior as play rather than real aggression or assertion. This matters for conversational humor and rough-and-tumble/performative comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conversational-maxim violations as mechanisms (Gricean moves)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor often depends on deliberately breaking conversational rules: Do not say what you believe to be false; Do not say that for which you lack adequate evidence; Avoid obscurity; Avoid ambiguity; Be brief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific violations produce different effects: breaking the truth rule by exaggeration (hyperbole), presenting fantasies as facts, using obscurity or ambiguity to confuse then reveal a punch line, or violating brevity to produce comic rants. Use these categories to analyze conversational jokes and stand-up techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linguistic ambiguity / double-meaning (wordplay/puns)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many jokes exploit shifts in meaning (ambiguity) so that the punch line forces a reinterpretation of earlier material (e.g., 'institution' in Mae West).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating wordplay, look for a clear, recoverable alternate parsing or meaning and a moment of reinterpretation that yields the pleasure of 'getting' the joke; absence of that recovery suggests merely confusing or obscure phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ethical constraint: harm and trivialization
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can be morally objectionable when it perpetuates stereotypes or treats subjects that should be taken seriously as objects for play, thereby blocking compassion and responsible action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a joke keeps harmful stereotypes 'in circulation' or trivializes real suffering (e.g., insensitive satire of famine). Consider social context and potential reinforcement of prejudice when judging moral acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional/therapeutic value
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor can foster tolerance for ambiguity and diversity, promote creative problem-solving, serve as a social lubricant (engender trust, reduce conflict), and reduce stress and its physiological consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these functions as positive evaluative criteria: does the humor increase social bonding, reduce negative emotions in delicate communications, or contribute to mental flexibility? Empirical claims (stress reduction, immune benefits) may be cited to justify the social/therapeutic value of humor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre/structural features of comedy (vs. tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy typically embodies an anti-heroic, pragmatic attitude: more everyday characters, common speech, emphasis on groups/families rather than lone heroes, emotional disengagement and thinking rather than feeling, and methods like trickery or deal-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a comic work, check for these formal and thematic markers (character types, language level, problem-solving tactics) to determine whether it aligns with comedic conventions and what kind of attitude toward incongruity it models.
